healthcareSolutions.title: Healthcare Solutions (Stericycle) revenue
healthcareSolutions.content:
Revenue from the Healthcare Solutions segment -- regulated medical waste, hazardous waste and secure document destruction, acquired with Stericycle in November 2024 for $7.2bn.

For Waste Management, Inc.: FY2024's $403m is only the two months since close; FY2025's $2,508m is the first full year and the number to judge the deal against. Quarterly run-rate since has held near $610-650m, i.e. roughly $2.5bn annualised -- management's case for the deal is cost synergies (route density, fewer disposal sites) lifting this segment's margin toward the legacy solid-waste business over time, not revenue growth from it.

What to watch:

  • Segment margin converging toward core collection & disposal margins as synergies are realised
  • Organic growth in the segment once the acquired base anniversarises (FY2026 onward)
  • Integration costs still flowing through corporate/other and depressing consolidated margins

lobRevenue.title: Revenue by line of business
lobRevenue.content:
Collection & disposal revenue split by customer type: Residential (municipal and subscription routes), Commercial (dumpster/front-load service to businesses), Industrial (roll-off and large-container), and Landfill (tipping fees, including third-party waste).

For Waste Management, Inc.: Commercial is the largest and stickiest of the four (long-term contracts, high switching cost) and the one management points to for pricing power; Industrial is the most cyclical, tracking construction and manufacturing activity.

What to watch:

  • Commercial growing faster than Industrial (resilience vs cyclicality)
  • Landfill revenue versus internal tons (pricing vs volume)

yield.title: Average yield and internal growth
yield.content:
Average yield is the price increase on existing collection & disposal volume, net of fuel/environmental surcharges -- WM's core pricing-power metric. Internal growth (also called volume growth) is the organic change in tons/units collected, excluding acquisitions.

For Waste Management, Inc.: the investment thesis rests on yield consistently outrunning WM's own cost inflation (a pricing algorithm applied disproportionately to low-margin, hard-to-service accounts); yield has been compressing over FY2022-FY2025 (6.7% to 3.8% on a collection & disposal basis) as the post-COVID inflation surge fades, with a pickup into FY2026 (up to 5.1% by Q3) worth tracking against cost trends.

What to watch:

  • Yield holding above cost inflation (fuel, labor, disposal)
  • Internal growth turning negative (volume losses, e.g. from pricing discipline shedding low-margin accounts)

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Waste Management, Inc.: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Waste Management, Inc.: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Waste Management, Inc.: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Waste Management, Inc.: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Waste Management, Inc.: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Waste Management, Inc.: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Waste Management, Inc.: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Waste Management, Inc.: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Waste Management, Inc.: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Waste Management, Inc.: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
